clue.text: A breeze, even at sea

parts.note: plain = level, even, said of ground with no bumps in it
a ship at sea is sailing

explanation.surface: A light wind blowing over calm open water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A breeze' looks like more weather, part of the same calm scene, when it is the definition — anything easy. Both halves of the wordplay are plain-English synonyms rather than crossword conventions, so there is nothing to decode, only to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything effortless is 'a breeze', and plain sailing is the matching idiom for a job with nothing in its way.

clue.text: Piano heavenly maiden keeps up for English lord

parts.note: P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

indicators.note: the heavenly word holds the next part inside it

parts.note: ethereal means heavenly, celestial

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: M is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: A soft-playing pianist keeps a celestial young woman awake for an English nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavenly maiden' tempts you to look for an angel or houri, but the words split: heavenly is the container and maiden is the cricketer's M, a maiden being an over with no runs scored.
explanation.definitionFit: A peer of the realm is a member of the British nobility, a duke, earl or baron entitled to sit in the House of Lords.

clue.text: Distributor of loaves and fishes has job dividing drink

indicators.note: what divides a word comes down in the middle of it and splits it in two

parts.note: ale is the drink, split to take the insertion
a post is a job, as in a teaching post

explanation.surface: A food supplier whose job also involves portioning out the drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: The loaves and fishes give the clue its religious pull, while the wordplay underneath is entirely secular — a job and a drink. Bible knowledge only helps with the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In the feeding of the five thousand the apostles take the bread and fish and hand them round the crowd.

clue.text: Feeling less clear about seat of power

parts.note: number, rhyming with plumber, means more numb, so feeling less

indicators.note: about in the sense of turned about, so the word for clear runs backwards

parts.note: net means clear, as in net profit after deductions

explanation.surface: Sensing less certainty about where authority sits.
explanation.walkthrough: NUMBER here is numb-er, more numb. Number Ten Downing Street is the British Prime Minister's residence and office.
explanation.definitionFit: Number Ten is shorthand for the British Prime Minister's official home, the centre of government power.

clue.text: African running along behind American on the outside

indicators.note: the reworked letters come behind, after, the pair from American
only the outside letters, the first and last, of American are used

parts.note: the first and last letters of American

indicators.note: the letters of along run about into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A runner from Africa trails an American on the outside lane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the outside' takes AN from American, and 'running' rearranges ALONG to GOLAN, placed 'behind' it. The race-track picture hides that American gives only its ends.
explanation.definitionFit: An Angolan is a person from Angola, a country in south-west Africa.

clue.text: Lineker's predecessor left a lot of people upset

indicators.note: something upset has been tipped over, and in a down entry that means its letters read up the column

parts.note: many = a lot of people, tipped over
l = left, as in stage directions

explanation.surface: The man before Lineker walked away and a lot of fans took it badly.
explanation.walkthrough: Presenters change chairs often enough that the surface passes as a news line, and both halves of it — the leaving and the upset — turn out to be letter instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: Des Lynam fronted the BBC's Saturday-night football highlights show Match of the Day until 1999, when Gary Lineker took the chair from him.

clue.text: GI's head treated by Spooner in surgery

indicators.note: Spooner, the Oxford don who swapped the opening sounds of words, gets to work on the phrase

parts.note: a GI, an American soldier, is a G.I. Joe, so GI's gives Joe's
nob is slang for the head

explanation.surface: An American soldier's head wound is treated in an operating theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: GI's head reads as JOE'S NOB; 'treated by Spooner' swaps the J and N sounds to give a phrase pronounced NOSE JOB. A GI Joe is an American private.
explanation.definitionFit: A nose job is informal for rhinoplasty, cosmetic or corrective surgery to reshape the nose.

clue.text: White lioness wandering across street? One changes sides in case

indicators.note: a wandering animal keeps to no fixed path, and these letters keep to no fixed order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters
st = street in any address

explanation.surface: An escaped white lioness padding across a suburban street.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is doing real work: a white lioness in the road is a picture you are meant to distrust. Everything after it is definition, not the single word 'case'.
explanation.definitionFit: A hostile witness turns on the side that called them to the stand, so the phrase describes someone switching allegiance in the middle of a trial.

clue.text: Certainly, marines get out of shape

parts.note: defo is British slang for definitely
RM = the Royal Marines, Britain's naval infantry

explanation.surface: Marines, of all people, letting their fitness go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get out of shape' is a gym complaint on the surface and geometry in the answer — something bent out of true. The slang 'defo' is spoken and texted rather than written formally, which is why 'certainly' stands in for it.
explanation.definitionFit: To deform a thing is to push it out of its proper shape, which is 'get out of shape' read literally.

clue.text: Scouts' cabaret jokes involving new method

indicators.note: to involve something is to wrap it up in what you are already doing, so it goes inside

parts.note: gags = jokes, opened up to take a letter
n = new, the standard abbreviation
the how of a thing is the method of doing it

explanation.surface: A Scout troop's comedy routine being tried out a new way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How' as a noun for method is the kind of everyday word setters lean on. The definition is the two words at the front, which read instead as a description of whose jokes these are.
explanation.definitionFit: A Gang Show is the Scouts' own variety concert, staged in British towns since 1932 and still an annual fixture.

clue.text: Place where you need English and French both strange et normal

definitions.text: Place where you need English and French

indicators.note: 'strange' means out of its proper order, and 'both' hands that treatment to each of the two words that follow

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: A town where getting by takes two languages, one of them leaking into the other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Et' is French for 'and', so the fodder itself is half in each language — the joke the surface is making about the place. Reading those two words as French is optional; the letters come out the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Montreal is Quebec's largest city, French-speaking by law and anglophone by habit, so both languages are in daily use there.

clue.text: Cocktail has oomph with vermouth added in

indicators.note: adding something in puts it inside what is already in the glass, not alongside it

parts.note: mojo = oomph, personal magic
Italian vermouth is 'it' in British bar shorthand, as in gin and it

explanation.surface: A barman livening up a drink with a slug of vermouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gin and it' was the standard order for gin with Italian vermouth, and that two-letter 'it' has outlived the drink by half a century in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A mojito is the Cuban mix of white rum, lime, sugar and mint, so 'Cocktail' is the straight category word for it.

clue.text: Spot last year's swallows

indicators.note: what swallows a thing keeps it whole inside, letters and order intact

parts.note: running across the join of laST YEar's

explanation.surface: Trying to catch sight of the swallows that nested here last year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swallows' is a bird on the surface and a verb underneath, which is why the eye slides straight past it. 'Spot' hides the same way, reading as looking rather than as a blemish.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is the small inflamed swelling on an eyelid — a spot in the everyday pimple sense.

clue.text: Fairy made from stone by the roadside to fill order

indicators.note: filling something means going inside it, so these pieces land within the word rather than beside it

parts.note: to tell someone to do something is to order them; the word opens up to be filled
a statue in marble is made from marble, so 'made from' = in
the kerb, spelt that way in Britain, is the stone edging between pavement and road

explanation.surface: A stonemason's roadside fairy, carved to fill a customer's order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' reads as the commission the mason is working on, and it is the word being filled — as a verb it means to tell. Two short pieces go in together, which is what buries the split.
explanation.definitionFit: Tinker Bell is Peter Pan's fairy, so the bare word 'Fairy' points at the most famous one by name.

clue.text: City in the Champions League playing in Devon, eh?

indicators.note: letters at play are letters on the move, and none of them stays where it was put

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A Champions League side turning out for a fixture down in Devon.
explanation.walkthrough: Devon is the county in England's far south-west, about as far from European football as you can get. The 'eh?' reads as the setter nudging you when it is really two more letters of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Eindhoven is the Dutch city whose club PSV is a regular in the Champions League, so the definition names it by its football.

clue.text: Sickly youth drinking etc, a boozy mess

indicators.note: to drink a thing is to take it inside you, so what follows goes within

parts.note: wan = pale and sickly; the word is opened up
the abbreviation taken exactly as written
a teen is a youth

explanation.surface: A pale teenager drinking and making a sorry, boozy mess of himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mess' is the word to re-read: not a shambles but the forces' dining room, and a wet one serves alcohol where a dry one does not. The drunk teenager of the surface is pure decoration.
explanation.definitionFit: In the British forces a wet canteen is the bar-serving mess, the place where drink is allowed.

clue.text: Dry sausage caught by software that's unreliable, mostly

parts.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

indicators.note: most of the software's name is used: it loses its last letter

parts.note: Horizon is the faulty IT system at the heart of the British Post Office scandal

explanation.surface: A cured sausage gets snagged by glitchy computer code.
explanation.walkthrough: Horizon was the Fujitsu accounting software whose false shortfalls led to hundreds of British sub-postmasters being wrongly prosecuted. 'Mostly' drops its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Chorizo is a spicy Spanish pork sausage, usually cured and air-dried rather than cooked.

clue.text: Ban consequently restricts doctor back in Chattanooga

indicators.note: to restrict something is to close round it and hold it in

parts.note: ergo = therefore, consequently; it opens to take the insertion
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is the standard British medical degree

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter, the one at the rear

parts.note: the letter at the back of Chattanooga

explanation.surface: A ban hemming in a doctor back home in Chattanooga.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is usually an instruction to jumble letters and here it is a straight abbreviation, which is the trap. Chattanooga, the Tennessee city of the Glenn Miller song, is in the clue for its last letter alone.
explanation.definitionFit: An embargo is an official bar on trade with a country, so 'Ban' is the plain noun for one.

clue.text: Small beard cut with teeth

parts.note: s = small, the clothing size
the awn is the bristly beard on an ear of barley or grass

explanation.surface: A little beard being trimmed with something toothed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beard' is the botanist's word here, the bristle on an ear of barley, and it comes up often enough to be worth keeping. The definition describes what a toothed blade leaves behind, not what a barber does.
explanation.definitionFit: Timber cut by a toothed blade has been sawn, the past participle the definition's own phrasing calls for.

clue.text: Uranium in anti-aircraft missile curtailed sortie for old fighter

indicators.note: the element is placed between the other pieces

parts.note: a SAM is a surface-to-air missile

indicators.note: cut short at the tail, so the last letter goes

parts.note: a raid is a sortie, an attack mission
U is the chemical symbol for uranium

explanation.surface: A nuclear-tipped missile is fired on a shortened mission.
explanation.walkthrough: The military surface hides a plain sequence: the missile, then the element, then the shortened mission, with 'in' slotting the element between them.
explanation.definitionFit: The samurai were the hereditary warrior class of feudal Japan, so fighters of old.

clue.text: Bang on target for ship in a storm?

parts.note: re = on, on the subject of, as in a memo heading

parts.words: target for ship in a storm
parts.note: a ship caught in a storm makes for port

explanation.surface: A shot dead on target, aimed at the haven a ship runs for in a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bang on' is the trap: read together the two words mean exactly right, and only the first of them is the definition. The question mark covers 'target' as a loose way of describing a harbour.
explanation.definitionFit: The report of a gun is the bang it makes, a noun sense that survives mainly in shooting and in crosswords.

clue.text: Championship belt Italian holds aloft

indicators.note: what holds a thing has it inside, whole and unbroken
a down entry is written downwards, so anything held aloft has to be read the other way, upwards

parts.note: reading up the column from the middle of bELT ITalian

explanation.surface: An Italian boxer lifting the championship belt above his head.
explanation.walkthrough: The boxing picture is exact — in the ring the belt is the championship — which is why the definition sits so quietly beside it. Hidden answers that run backwards are the hardest kind to catch.
explanation.definitionFit: Winning a championship is winning the title, the word used for the honour itself in boxing and most other sports.

clue.text: Great being hot, covered with insects

indicators.note: a cover goes over a thing on both sides, leaving it hidden inside

parts.note: a bee is the first of the insects, split to cover the letter
h = hot, as marked on a tap
a moth is the second of them

explanation.surface: Someone sweltering in the heat and crawling with bugs.
explanation.walkthrough: One plural, 'insects', has to be read as two separate creatures, and that is the whole difficulty of the charade. The 'great being' of the definition is the beast of the Book of Job, which is where English took the word from.
explanation.definitionFit: A behemoth is a creature of enormous size, named in the Book of Job, and the word still covers anything huge.

clue.text: Flog relics to monastery

indicators.note: to flog is to beat, and a beating knocks the letters clean out of their order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: Selling off a load of holy relics to a monastery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flog' reads as selling, which is just what you would do with relics, and only its other sense of whipping gives the instruction. 'To' looks like a joining word and is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A cloister is the covered walk at the heart of a monastery and, by extension, the monastery itself — the sense in 'a cloistered life'.

clue.text: Monkey really having tail clipped by horse-doctor?

indicators.note: the word for really loses its last letter

parts.note: very means really, as in really good
a vet treats animals, horses included

explanation.surface: A monkey's tail is docked by a vet who normally treats horses.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags horse-doctor as a playful way of describing a vet. 'Having tail clipped' acts on the word for really, not on the monkey.
explanation.definitionFit: The vervet is a small black-faced African monkey with greyish fur.

clue.text: Wrecked Syrian city contains green and free area in SE

indicators.note: the city's name holds the following pieces inside it

parts.note: Homs, a Syrian city badly damaged in the civil war
eco- is the prefix for environmentally friendly, green
to untie is to free

explanation.surface: A war-ravaged Syrian city holds a green, liberated region in the south-east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrecked' describes the city, not an anagram. The Home Counties are the English counties surrounding London.
explanation.definitionFit: The Home Counties are the counties around London, such as Surrey and Kent, in the south-east of England.
